about: On-board parts of common microcontroller boards for Circuit Lab's Inspect mode: what each part is, where it sits, its role on this board, key specs, the nets it touches, and a kid-friendly line plus a deeper explanation (from its kind). Guide: knowledge/board-teardown.md.
units: Millimetres. Board origin at the lower-left corner seen from the component side; x to the right, y up (as in the design files). w/d = part footprint along its own x/y before rotation; rot = degrees counter-clockwise; h = height above the board; z = extra base height when a part sits on another; side = top | bottom.
rules: Specs come from datasheets or the maker's BOM; nothing is guessed silently — estimated positions and inferred nets are flagged per board (positions) and per part (note).
No company logos: only the part markings needed to teach (e.g. "ESP32-WROOM-32", "AMS1117 3.3").

mcu.label: Microcontroller
mcu.kid: The brain of the board: it reads your program and switches its pins on and off millions of times a second.
mcu.deep: A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip: a CPU core, flash memory that keeps the program, RAM for variables, and peripherals (timers, ADC, UART, SPI, I²C, PWM) routed to the pins through multiplexers. Each GPIO is a push-pull CMOS stage — a P-MOSFET to the supply and an N-MOSFET to ground — that can also become a high-impedance input with an optional internal pull-up. The crystal or resonator beside it sets the clock, and the small capacitors around it supply the current spikes every clock edge draws.
facts: A pin is a signal, not a power supply: it can source or sink only a few tens of milliamps before it is damaged.
Most of the other parts on the board exist only to power, clock, reset and program this one chip.
misconceptions: "The whole board is the microcontroller." The board is a carrier; the chip is the microcontroller, and the rest feeds it power, a clock and a USB link.

usb-uart.label: USB-to-serial bridge
usb-uart.kid: The translator: it turns USB messages from your computer into simple serial signals the brain understands.
usb-uart.deep: USB 2.0 full speed sends packets at 12 Mbit/s on a differential pair (D+ and D−). Many microcontrollers only speak UART: one wire out (TX), one wire in (RX), a start bit, 8 data bits and a stop bit. The bridge enumerates as a serial port on your computer, buffers bytes both ways, and also drives the modem lines DTR and RTS, which the board uses to reset the microcontroller into its bootloader when you upload.
facts: Every Serial.print travels: your code → UART TX → this chip → USB → the Serial Monitor.
The TX/RX LEDs blink when bytes pass through this chip.
misconceptions: "Serial pins are free to use." The board's RX/TX pins are wired to this bridge; using them for something else can break uploads and the Serial Monitor.

rf-module.label: Radio module
rf-module.kid: A tiny radio station in a metal box: the chip, its memory and its antenna, tested and certified together.
rf-module.deep: An RF module puts the wireless microcontroller die, its crystal, the SPI flash that holds your program and the RF matching network under a metal shield can, next to a printed antenna on the module's own PCB. Because the radio is certified as a module (the IDs printed on the can), the board around it does not need its own radio certification. The castellated pads around the edge carry the GPIOs, power and the flash bus.
facts: The metal can is a shield against radio interference, not a heatsink.
Keep metal and ground copper away from the antenna end or the Wi-Fi range drops.
misconceptions: "The metal can is the chip." The chip is underneath it, beside the flash memory and the crystal.

antenna.label: PCB antenna
antenna.kid: The wiggly gold line is the Wi-Fi antenna — it is just copper drawn in a special shape.
antenna.deep: A meandered inverted-F antenna (MIFA): a quarter-wave resonator for 2.4 GHz (λ/4 ≈ 31 mm in air, shorter on FR-4 because the board material slows the wave), folded to fit. One end is grounded and the feed taps in near it to match 50 Ω. It needs a keep-out area with no copper under or beside it, which is why it hangs at the end of the board.
facts: 2.4 GHz waves are about 12.5 cm long; the antenna is a fraction of that, tuned by its length.
misconceptions: "It is a broken trace that goes nowhere." It is meant to end in the air: that open end is where it radiates.

ldo.label: Linear regulator (LDO)
ldo.kid: The voltage step-down: it takes a higher voltage and gives out a steady, lower one for the chips.
ldo.deep: A linear regulator is a pass transistor driven by an error amplifier that compares the output (through a divider) with an internal reference of about 1.25 V. It burns the difference as heat: P = (Vin − Vout) × I. Dropout is the smallest Vin − Vout at which it still regulates. It needs capacitors on its input and output, and many are only stable with output capacitors in a certain ESR range.
facts: From 12 V down to 5 V at 0.5 A, a linear regulator turns 3.5 W into heat — enough to make a small package shut down.
misconceptions: "A regulator can raise the voltage too." A linear regulator only steps down; stepping up needs a switching (boost) converter.

buck-boost.label: Buck-boost converter
buck-boost.kid: A clever power converter: whether the battery is above or below 3.3 V, it makes exactly 3.3 V without wasting much.
buck-boost.deep: A switch-mode buck-boost converter chops current through an inductor about a million times a second with four internal switches. Storing energy in the inductor's magnetic field and releasing it with a controlled duty cycle lets it step down (buck) or up (boost) at around 90 % efficiency instead of burning the difference as heat. At light load it can skip pulses (PFM) to save power at the cost of more ripple.
facts: The Pico runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V on VSYS — two AA cells or a LiPo cell both work.
misconceptions: "Switching supplies are too noisy for sensors." The ripple is small; forcing PWM mode (GPIO23 high on the Pico) lowers it further for ADC readings.

flash.label: Flash memory
flash.kid: The notebook where your program is saved, even when the power is off.
flash.deep: NOR flash stores each bit as charge trapped on a floating-gate transistor, so it keeps data without power for decades and survives about 100,000 erase cycles per sector. Quad-SPI moves 4 bits per clock; the microcontroller can run code straight out of it (execute in place) through a small cache.
facts: 16 Mbit = 2 MB: room for your program plus a small file system.
misconceptions: "Flash is the same as RAM." RAM forgets everything at power-off and is much faster to write; flash keeps data but must be erased in blocks before rewriting.

crystal.label: Quartz crystal
crystal.kid: The heartbeat: a tiny slice of quartz that wiggles at an exact speed so the chip keeps perfect time.
crystal.deep: Quartz is piezoelectric — voltage bends it and bending makes voltage. Cut to size, it resonates mechanically at one frequency with a quality factor above 10,000; the chip's inverting amplifier and two load capacitors (a Pierce oscillator) keep it ringing. Typical accuracy is ±20–50 ppm, a couple of seconds a day.
facts: USB needs an accurate clock (±0.25 %), which is why the USB chip gets a real crystal.
misconceptions: "The clock speed is set in software only." Software can divide or multiply it with a PLL, but this part is the reference everything is counted from.

resonator.label: Ceramic resonator
resonator.kid: A cheaper heartbeat made of ceramic: it ticks 16 million times a second.
resonator.deep: A ceramic resonator works like a crystal but with lower Q and accuracy (about ±0.5 %), and it has the load capacitors built in, so it has three pins: two ends and ground. Fine for running a sketch, too loose for keeping precise time — millis() can drift by seconds an hour.
facts: ±0.5 % is 18 seconds an hour; a clock project on an Uno needs a real-time-clock module.
misconceptions: "16 MHz means 16 million instructions a second exactly." Most AVR instructions take one clock, but some take two to four.

cap-decoupling.label: Decoupling capacitor
cap-decoupling.kid: A tiny energy bucket right next to a chip, so the chip never runs short when it switches fast.
cap-decoupling.deep: Every clock edge a digital chip pulls a current spike lasting nanoseconds. The supply traces have inductance (roughly 1 nH per mm), so V = L·di/dt makes the rail dip. A 100 nF ceramic capacitor millimetres from the power pin supplies that charge locally and shorts high-frequency noise to ground. Rule of thumb: one 100 nF per power pin, as close as possible, plus a bulk capacitor nearby.
facts: Remove the decoupling capacitors and a board can still work on the bench — then crash randomly when a motor starts.
misconceptions: "Bigger capacitors are always better." Small ceramics work at high frequency because they have very little inductance; big ones cover slower dips. Boards use both.

cap-bulk.label: Bulk capacitor
cap-bulk.kid: A bigger energy bucket that keeps the power steady when something switches on.
cap-bulk.deep: Bulk capacitors (microfarads to tens of microfarads) hold a rail up during load steps and cover the slower part of the noise; regulators also need them to stay stable. Ceramic X5R capacitors lose much of their capacitance under DC bias — a 10 µF 6.3 V part may be nearer 4 µF at 5 V.
facts: A regulator without its output capacitor can oscillate and make a noisy supply out of a clean one.
misconceptions: "A capacitor is a tiny battery." It stores far less energy and gives it back in microseconds; its job is smoothing, not running the board.

cap-electrolytic.label: Electrolytic capacitor
cap-electrolytic.kid: A tall can of stored energy that steadies the power coming into the board.
cap-electrolytic.deep: An aluminium electrolytic capacitor uses a thin oxide film on etched foil as its dielectric, which gives a lot of capacitance in a small can — but it is polarised. Reversed, the oxide breaks down, gas builds up and the vent cut into the top opens. Its series resistance (ESR) helps damp ringing on the regulator input.
facts: The cross pressed into the top is a vent so a failing capacitor opens gently instead of bursting.
misconceptions: "Either way round is fine." Electrolytics have a − stripe; reversing them can make them bulge or vent.

cap-load.label: Crystal load capacitor
cap-load.kid: One of two tiny capacitors that help the crystal tick at exactly the right speed.
cap-load.deep: The oscillator sees the two capacitors in series, plus stray board capacitance, as the crystal's load: CL = C1·C2/(C1 + C2) + Cstray. The crystal is cut for one load value, and the wrong capacitors pull its frequency by tens of ppm or stop it starting.
facts: 22 pF + 22 pF in series is 11 pF; with ~5 pF of stray capacitance the crystal sees about 16 pF.
misconceptions: "Any small capacitor will do." The value is chosen from the crystal's datasheet.

cap-filter.label: Filter capacitor
cap-filter.kid: A small capacitor that smooths out noise on one wire.
cap-filter.deep: With a resistor in series (on the board or inside the chip) it forms an RC low-pass filter with a corner at f = 1/(2πRC): slow changes pass, fast noise is shunted to ground. Reference pins (AREF) and analog supply pins get one so the ADC reads steadier numbers.
facts: 10 kΩ and 100 nF make a filter at about 160 Hz.
misconceptions: "A filter capacitor removes all noise." It only removes noise above its corner frequency.

cap-coupling.label: Auto-reset capacitor
cap-coupling.kid: The trick that restarts the chip by itself when you click Upload.
cap-coupling.deep: A series capacitor passes changes but blocks steady levels. When the USB bridge drops DTR, the edge goes through this 100 nF capacitor and pulls RESET low for about a millisecond (τ = 10 kΩ × 100 nF = 1 ms) before the pull-up recharges it, so the bootloader starts just as the upload begins.
facts: Opening the Serial Monitor also toggles DTR — that is why the board restarts when you open it.
misconceptions: "The upload button presses reset over the cable." Nothing mechanical happens: one capacitor turns a USB control line into a short reset pulse.

resistor.label: Resistor
resistor.kid: A speed bump for electricity: it limits how much current can flow.
resistor.deep: Ohm's law: V = I·R. A thick-film chip resistor is resistive paste printed on a ceramic block with metal end caps; the printed code gives the value (103 = 10 × 10³ = 10 kΩ). Its power rating comes from its size — about 63 mW for 0402 and 100 mW for 0603.
facts: Some chip resistors are too small to print a code on; you need a multimeter or the BOM to know them.
misconceptions: "Resistors use up current." The same current flows in and out; a resistor turns some of the voltage into heat.

resistor-network.label: Resistor array
resistor-network.kid: Four resistors squeezed into one tiny part to save space.
resistor-network.deep: A resistor array puts four equal resistors side by side on one ceramic chip (CAY16/CAT16: 4 × 0603 in 3.2 × 1.6 mm) — one pick-and-place step instead of four, and matched values. Concave (CAY) and convex (CAT) terminations are two styles of the same idea.
facts: One array can serve four different jobs: two pull-ups and two LED resistors can share a part if they need the same value.
misconceptions: "It is one big resistor." It is four separate ones sharing a body.

resistor-pullup.label: Pull-up resistor
resistor-pullup.kid: It gently holds a wire HIGH so it does not float around when nothing is driving it.
resistor-pullup.deep: A floating CMOS input picks up noise and reads random values. A pull-up (often 10 kΩ) to the supply makes "high" the default; a button or transistor to ground overrides it while only 0.5 mA (5 V / 10 kΩ) flows.
facts: The "weak" internal pull-ups in microcontrollers are 20–50 kΩ.
misconceptions: "A pull-up makes the pin an output." The pin stays an input; the resistor just decides what it reads when nothing else does.

resistor-led.label: LED resistor
resistor-led.kid: It keeps the LED from getting too much current and burning out.
resistor-led.deep: An LED has almost no resistance once its forward voltage is reached, so a series resistor sets the current: I = (Vsupply − Vf) / R. With 5 V, a 2 V LED and 1 kΩ: (5 − 2) / 1000 = 3 mA — enough to see, easy on the pin.
facts: Indicator LEDs on boards run at a few milliamps; modern LEDs are bright at 2 mA.
misconceptions: "The resistor goes on the + side only." Either side works — the current is the same all round the loop.

resistor-series.label: Series resistor
resistor-series.kid: A small resistor in a signal wire that keeps the signal clean and protects the pins.
resistor-series.deep: Series resistors damp ringing on fast edges, match a driver to its trace (USB full speed needs about 45 Ω per line: the driver's own ~20 Ω plus 22–27 Ω), and limit the current if two outputs ever drive the same wire in opposite directions.
facts: On Arduino boards, the 1 kΩ resistors between the USB chip and D0/D1 let a shield on those pins win over the USB chip.
misconceptions: "Signal resistors waste the signal." The input of a chip draws almost no current, so the voltage arrives unchanged.

resistor-divider.label: Voltage divider resistor
resistor-divider.kid: With a partner resistor, it turns a big voltage into a smaller one the chip can measure.
resistor-divider.deep: Two resistors in series split a voltage: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). High values (tens to hundreds of kΩ) keep the current tiny, so the divider can stay connected all the time.
facts: 200 kΩ over 100 kΩ divides by 3: 5 V on VSYS reads as 1.67 V on the Pico's ADC3.
misconceptions: "A divider is a power supply." It only works into a high-impedance input; any real load changes its output.

resistor-bias.label: Oscillator bias resistor
resistor-bias.kid: It helps the crystal's amplifier wake up and start ticking.
resistor-bias.deep: A large resistor (1 MΩ) across the oscillator's inverting amplifier biases it into its linear region (input ≈ output ≈ half the supply), where it has gain, so oscillation can build up from noise at power-on.
facts: Many chips have this resistor inside; some boards add it outside for reliable starting.
misconceptions: "It sets the frequency." The crystal sets the frequency; the resistor only makes it start.

resistor-zero.label: Zero-ohm link
resistor-zero.kid: A "resistor" that is really just a wire — the factory uses it as a bridge.
resistor-zero.deep: A 0 Ω resistor is a jumper in a resistor's body, so the same pick-and-place machine can fit it. Designers use them to choose options at assembly time (fit or leave out), to hop a trace over another, or to leave a place to measure current.
facts: Its marking is a single 0.
misconceptions: "Zero ohms does nothing." It connects — leaving it out is what changes the circuit.

led.label: LED
led.kid: A tiny light that shows what is happening: power is on, data is moving, or your code is blinking it.
led.deep: A light-emitting diode glows when electrons and holes recombine across its junction; the colour comes from the band gap of the semiconductor (red about 1.8–2.1 V forward drop, green and blue about 2.8–3.3 V). It has almost no resistance above its forward voltage, so it always needs something to limit the current.
facts: A board's "L" or GPIO2 LED is the first thing most people ever program: Blink.
misconceptions: "LEDs work either way round." They only conduct and light from anode to cathode.

diode-schottky.label: Schottky diode
diode-schottky.kid: A one-way door for electricity, so power cannot flow backwards into your computer.
diode-schottky.deep: A Schottky diode is a metal–semiconductor junction: a low forward drop (0.3–0.5 V) and very fast switching. Between USB VBUS and the board's supply it lets USB power the board but stops an external supply on VIN or VSYS pushing current back into the USB port.
facts: Its drop is why a USB-powered board often measures 4.6–4.8 V on its "5V" pin.
misconceptions: "A diode has no voltage loss." Every diode drops some voltage while conducting — Schottkys just drop less.

diode-rectifier.label: Rectifier diode
diode-rectifier.kid: A one-way door that protects the board if a power plug is wired the wrong way round.
diode-rectifier.deep: A silicon PN rectifier (1 A, 1000 V reverse rating, about 1 V forward drop). If the barrel plug has reversed polarity the diode blocks, so no current flows and nothing is damaged. The price is about 1 V lost from VIN.
facts: The M7 is the surface-mount version of the classic 1N4007.
misconceptions: "Reverse polarity always destroys a board." Here this diode makes it a harmless mistake.

diode-clamp.label: Clamp diode
diode-clamp.kid: A safety valve that stops the reset pin seeing too much voltage.
diode-clamp.deep: When the auto-reset capacitor releases, the reset line can spike above the supply. The diode conducts into +5 V and clamps the line to about VCC + 0.7 V. It also keeps RESET from rising toward 12 V, which on an AVR means "enter high-voltage programming mode".
facts: The diode is a 1N4148-class small-signal diode in a glass MiniMELF body.
misconceptions: "Reset pins cannot be damaged." Spikes from the auto-reset circuit are exactly what this part is there for.

tvs-esd.label: ESD protector
tvs-esd.kid: A lightning rod for the USB wires: it soaks up the static zap from your fingers.
tvs-esd.deep: ESD suppressors (multilayer varistors or TVS diodes) stay high-resistance at normal voltages and conduct hard above their clamp voltage, dumping a static discharge of several kilovolts to ground in nanoseconds. Their low capacitance (under a picofarad) keeps the 12 Mbit/s USB signals clean.
facts: A spark you barely feel is about 3 kV; one you can see is over 8 kV.
misconceptions: "Static only matters in dry winters." Chips are damaged by discharges far too small for you to feel.

ferrite.label: Ferrite bead
ferrite.kid: A tiny bead that blocks electrical noise but lets steady current through.
ferrite.deep: A ferrite bead has almost no resistance at DC but hundreds of ohms at 100 MHz, where it turns radio-frequency noise into heat. Here it ties the USB connector's metal shield to the board's ground, so noise picked up by the cable does not flood the ground plane.
facts: A ferrite bead is also the lump you see on some USB and monitor cables.
misconceptions: "It is an inductor for power supplies." It is built to be lossy and waste noise as heat, not to store energy.

inductor.label: Power inductor
inductor.kid: A coil that stores energy in a magnetic field — the power converter's helper.
inductor.deep: In a switching converter the inductor carries the current between switch cycles and smooths it: V = L·di/dt. It is rated by its saturation current — above that the core cannot hold more field and the inductance collapses — and by its resistance (DCR), which costs efficiency.
facts: 2.2 µH with 2.7 A saturation fits in 2.5 × 2 mm thanks to a ferrite core around the winding.
misconceptions: "Coils are only for radios and motors." Every efficient phone or laptop power supply has one.

fuse-ptc.label: Resettable fuse
fuse-ptc.kid: A self-healing fuse: it stops too much current, then fixes itself when it cools down.
fuse-ptc.deep: A polymeric PTC fuse is carbon particles in a polymer. Too much current heats it; the polymer expands, the carbon paths break, and its resistance jumps by orders of magnitude so only a trickle flows. Remove the fault, let it cool, and it conducts again. It protects your computer's USB port from a short on the board.
facts: If a board "dies" after a short and comes back a minute later, this fuse tripped and reset.
misconceptions: "A fuse trips the instant you exceed its rating." PTCs trip in seconds at twice the hold current; brief peaks pass.

mosfet-p.label: P-channel MOSFET
mosfet-p.kid: An electric switch with no moving parts: pull its gate low and power flows through.
mosfet-p.deep: A MOSFET's gate is insulated; its voltage relative to the source forms or removes a conducting channel. A P-channel part conducts when its gate is pulled below its source, so it makes a good high-side power switch. Its on-resistance (RDS(on)) sets the loss: P = I²·R.
facts: At 0.5 A and 70 mΩ it wastes only 17.5 mW — far less than a diode would.
misconceptions: "A transistor needs current to stay on." A MOSFET gate draws essentially no steady current — just a little to charge it.

mosfet-n.label: N-channel MOSFET
mosfet-n.kid: A tiny electric switch: a voltage on its gate opens or closes a path for current.
mosfet-n.deep: An N-channel MOSFET conducts from drain to source when its gate is above its source by the threshold voltage (about 1 V for this small part). With no gate drive it blocks, which is how it can cut a leakage path when a supply is off.
facts: SOT-523 is 1.6 × 0.8 mm — smaller than a grain of rice.
misconceptions: "MOSFETs block both ways." Their body diode conducts in reverse; designers place them so that diode points the harmless way.

bjt.label: NPN transistor
bjt.kid: A tiny electronic switch turned on by a small current.
bjt.deep: An NPN bipolar transistor lets a collector current about 100× its base current flow; driven hard through a base resistor it acts as a switch. On ESP32 boards two of them are cross-wired so the USB bridge's DTR and RTS lines can pull EN and GPIO0 low in the right order — entering the bootloader without pressing BOOT — while both lines high or both low changes nothing.
facts: The marking "J3Y" on a SOT-23 is an S8050.
misconceptions: "The BOOT button is always needed to upload." The transistor pair does it for you; some boards need the button only because their EN capacitor is too small.

opamp.label: Op-amp / comparator
opamp.kid: A tiny comparing machine: it checks which of two voltages is bigger and acts on it.
opamp.deep: An op-amp amplifies the difference between its inputs about 100,000 times. With no feedback it slams to one rail or the other — a comparator. With its output wired back to its input it becomes a buffer that copies a voltage while drawing almost no current from the source.
facts: On the Uno and Mega one half of this chip decides between USB and external power; the other half lights the L LED from pin 13.
misconceptions: "Op-amps are only for audio." Here one is used as a power-path switch and an LED driver.

button.label: Push button
button.kid: Press it and two wires touch — to restart the board or choose how it starts.
button.deep: A tactile switch has a metal dome that snaps down to connect its contacts. The contacts bounce for 1–10 ms; an RC filter or software debounce handles that. With four legs, the legs come in pairs that are always connected inside.
facts: The reset button just pulls the reset pin to ground; the chip starts the program again when you let go.
misconceptions: "Reset erases the program." It only restarts it; the program stays in flash.

usb-connector.label: USB connector
usb-connector.kid: Where the cable plugs in: it brings power (5 V) and data from your computer.
usb-connector.deep: USB 2.0 has four wires: VBUS (5 V, up to 500 mA from a computer port), D+, D− and ground (micro and mini add an ID pin). Data is differential: the receiver looks at D+ minus D−, so noise that hits both wires equally cancels out. The metal shell is grounded through the board to keep radio noise in check.
facts: Some cables carry only power; if a board will not show up as a port, try a data cable.
misconceptions: "A bigger USB plug gives more power." The connector shape does not set the current; the port and the board do.

dc-jack.label: Barrel jack
dc-jack.kid: The round socket for a wall adapter or battery pack.
dc-jack.deep: A 2.1 mm centre-positive barrel jack. Its voltage goes through a protection diode to VIN and then to the 5 V regulator; 7–12 V is the comfortable range: lower and the regulator drops out, higher and it overheats.
facts: A 9 V battery works, but only for a few hours — it holds little energy.
misconceptions: "Any adapter that fits is safe." The polarity and voltage must match: centre +, 7–12 V.

header.label: Pin header
header.kid: Rows of holes (or pins) where you plug your wires in.
header.deep: Headers are on a 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) grid — the same as a breadboard. Each contact is a metal pin soldered to a trace that leads to a chip pin or a power rail; the label printed beside it tells you which.
facts: Female headers on an Uno are why shields stack on top of it.
misconceptions: "All pins are the same." Some are power, some are ground, some are special (reset, reference) — read the label first.

header-icsp.label: ICSP header
header-icsp.kid: A programming plug for experts: a special programmer can write straight into the chip through it.
header-icsp.deep: ICSP (In-Circuit Serial Programming) brings out MISO, MOSI, SCK, RESET, VCC and GND — the AVR's SPI programming interface. It is used to burn the bootloader, or to program the chip with no bootloader at all; shields also use it to reach SPI on any board.
facts: Pin 1 is marked with a dot or a thicker outline; plugging a programmer in rotated is a common mistake.
misconceptions: "You need ICSP to upload sketches." Normal uploads go over USB through the bootloader.

solder-jumper.label: Solder jumper
solder-jumper.kid: Two little pads joined by a thin bridge you can cut with a knife to change how the board behaves.
solder-jumper.deep: A solder jumper is a short copper link meant to be cut, or a gap meant to be bridged with solder. It sets an option forever without adding a switch.
facts: Cutting RESET-EN stops the board restarting every time a computer opens its serial port.
misconceptions: "Cutting a trace ruins the board." This one is designed to be cut — and can be bridged again with solder.

empty-footprint.label: Empty footprint
empty-footprint.kid: An empty parking spot: a place for a part the factory chose not to fit.
empty-footprint.deep: Designers leave pads for optional parts so one PCB can be built in several versions — a different module, a debug connector, or a part only needed for testing.
facts: Look for pads with no part on them: they often hint at hidden features.
misconceptions: "A missing part means the board is broken." Not-fitted parts are planned.

pads.label: Pads
pads.kid: Flat gold spots on the board where wires or test probes can touch.
pads.deep: Exposed copper pads, gold-plated (ENIG) so they do not tarnish. Castellated edge pads are holes cut in half, so the whole board can be soldered flat onto another board like a chip.
facts: The Pico can be soldered directly onto a bigger board using its castellated edge.
misconceptions: "Pads are decoration." Each one is a real connection to a net.

boards.name: ESP32 DevKit V1 (30 pins)
boards.summary: The common 30-pin ESP32 board (DOIT layout): an ESP32-WROOM-32 module, a CP2102 USB-to-serial chip, an AMS1117 3.3 V regulator and the auto-program transistors.
boards.positionsNote: DOIT never published design files. Part positions are our estimates from photos and the 51 × 28 mm outline (pin rows 0.9″ apart, matching Circuit Lab's 3D model); reference designators are our own labels. The circuit follows Espressif's ESP32-DevKitC V4 reference schematic, which these boards copy. Clones vary: some use a CH340C or CH9102X instead of the CP2102.

parts.name: ESP32-WROOM-32 module
parts.role: The brain and the radio: the ESP32 chip, 4 MB flash, a 40 MHz crystal and the antenna, under one shield can.

specs.Peak current: about 500 mA during Wi-Fi transmit bursts

facts: Wi-Fi transmit bursts draw up to ~500 mA for a few ms — a weak USB cable or supply makes the board reset ("brownout detector was triggered").
GPIO 6–11 are wired to the flash inside the module, which is why this board does not break them out.
misconceptions: "The ESP32 is 5 V like an Arduino." Its pins are 3.3 V; 5 V on a GPIO can damage it.
